name: Counselor Jess

inspiration.oldScript: Friday the 13th made sex a death sentence: skinny-dippers and counselors who fool around get killed, all because a drowned boy's avenging mother blamed the teens who looked away.
inspiration.newLens: Jess is a drowned girl the counselors ignored and the grown-ups failed, while the town has blamed "boy-crazy teen girls" ever since and forgotten her name. The skinny-dippers turn out to be helpers, the director who cut the lifeguard is named, and the crew wins by getting in the water with her so she learns she is not alone.

logline: Every night this week the drained quarry lake comes back to Crystal Street, a little deeper each time, and out of the moonlit water wades a towering woman in a torn navy dress and a cracked hockey mask, machete in hand, enforcing camp rules on every teenager she catches not watching.
backstory: Before Crystal Street existed, the land under it was the Crystal Springs quarry lake, and on its shore stood Camp Crystal Pines. In August 1957 twelve-year-old Jessamyn "Jess" Mercer was the most enthusiastic camper there: tin whistle, borrowed clipboard, a hand-me-down navy counselor's dress her mother had taken in, and a habit of reminding everyone of the rules. She wanted to be a counselor more than anything. She also could not swim. Three times she asked the junior counselors to teach her, and three times they said tomorrow; the director, Harlan Pratt, told her to stop pestering the big kids, because girls her age only wanted attention. So she pencilled SWIMMER over BEGINNER on her own swim card. On the last night of camp Pratt saved on staff by leaving two sixteen-year-old junior counselors, Judy Kessler and Bobby Teague, alone with forty kids at the night swim, no lifeguard, while he played poker in the lodge. The two teens looked away for one minute, at each other. Jess swam for the raft to prove she belonged. Afterward Pratt told the newspaper his girl counselor had been "boy-crazy," and the whole county agreed. Bobby went off to college. Judy became a cautionary tale, and the county printed a swim-safety poster that has hung in every school since: EYES ON THE WATER, GIRLS. NOT ON THE BOYS. Jess's name is nowhere on it. Two years later the lake was drained and Crystal Street was built on the lakebed. Now the Heartstone has called the water back, and Jess with it, grown in death into the counselor nobody would let her be: a towering, muscular woman in that navy dress, torn and laced up the front, long dark hair streaming lake water, quarry-rock scars stitched up her arms and thigh, a camp machete in her fist, and a cracked hockey mask she pulls on whenever she remembers that the town only ever saw a monster at the lake. Her voice still cracks like a twelve-year-old's.

centralIssue.title: Neglect, and blaming the girls
centralIssue.summary: Jess was not a cautionary tale, and the girl on the dock was not the reason she drowned. A grown-up left kids in charge of kids, then blamed a sixteen-year-old girl for being boy-crazy, and the town has been warning its daughters ever since while forgetting the drowned girl's name. Jess rages at every teen who looks away, and she wears the mask the town handed her, but what she never had was someone who would get in the water with her. Find her swim card, hear Judy's side and learn what her mother wrote, then say her name and teach her she is not alone in the water.

poster: A towering, muscular adult woman with long dark wavy hair streaming lake water, pulling a cracked hockey-style mask over her face with one hand, wearing a soaked, torn, high-necked navy camp-staff dress with short sleeves and a tin whistle on a lanyard, a dull rusty machete held low and pointed at the ground in her other hand, standing in tall reeds on a moonlit lakeshore beside a wooden dock, an empty swim raft on the silver water, a lit cabin across the lake, a cooler, folding chairs, an inner tube and towels on the grass, a full moon over dark pines
portrait: Close portrait of a towering, muscular woman lifting a cracked hockey-style mask off her face to reveal wide, hurt eyes much younger than the rest of her, freckles on lake-pale skin, long dark wavy hair dripping water, a soaked high-necked navy camp-staff dress with a tin whistle on a lanyard, lit by moonlight and a teal glow from the water below
endingPhoto: A towering, muscular woman with long wet dark hair pulling a cracked hockey-style mask over her face at the edge of a moonlit lake, a soaked high-necked navy camp-staff dress and a tin whistle on a lanyard, a dull rusty machete pointed at the ground, teens in pajamas and sweatshirts fleeing up the shore toward a lit cabin, coolers, towels and a folding chair scattered across the grass, pines under a huge moon
taunts: Buddy check! Where's your buddy? Nobody? Figures.
Rule number one: it's always the girls' fault. Everybody says so.
I passed my swim test. I passed it. I PASSED IT.
Say my name. Go on. Nobody in this town ever does.

clues.title: Jess's swim card
clues.hint: When Camp Crystal Pines was torn down, its office trailer and campers' footlockers were hauled to Rusty's Junkyard.

encounter.title: Lost and Found, 1957
encounter.place: A rusted camp office trailer, Rusty's Junkyard
encounter.text: Deep in the car maze, half swallowed by blackberry bushes, sits a mint-green trailer with CAMP CRYSTAL PINES OFFICE still stenciled on the door. Inside: bunk lists, a rack of rotted life jackets and a stack of camper footlockers. One has a name in careful block letters: J. MERCER, FUTURE COUNSELOR. A puddle of lake water spreads slowly out from under it, though it has not rained in weeks.
encounter.art: A rusted mint-green camp office trailer half swallowed by blackberry brambles deep in a junkyard car maze, its door hanging open, inside a rack of rotted orange life jackets, bunk lists pinned to a corkboard and a stack of dented camper footlockers, a slow puddle of lake water spreading across the floor from under the bottom footlocker, a teenager crouching in the doorway, dusty afternoon sun through grimy windows, medium wide shot

choices.label: Pop the footlocker's rusted latch

success.text: The latch gives with a gasp of damp air. A tin whistle. A clipboard with rules copied in a girl's round handwriting. A letter never mailed: Dear Mom, I asked Judy and Bobby three times to teach me to swim and they said tomorrow. Mr. Pratt says girls my age only want to hang around the big kids. I told them I can swim so I can do the night swim. I'll figure it out. Don't tell Dad. And the swim card: BEGINNER, DOES NOT SWIM, with SWIMMER pencilled over it, pressed so hard it tore.
success.art: An open camper footlocker in a junkyard trailer holding a tin whistle, a child's handwritten clipboard, an unmailed letter and a swim card with a word pencilled over the official stamp

failure.text: The latch snaps back on your fingers and the footlocker floods from the inside, lake water pouring out across the trailer floor, cold and smelling of pine needles. Somewhere behind you, very close, a whistle blows one long blast, and something heavy and sharp drags along the trailer's outside wall. You get out fast.
failure.art: Dark lake water gushing out of a closed footlocker across a trailer floor, a teen bolting out of the door into moonlight, the shadow of a tall figure with a machete on the trailer wall

choices.label: Go through the camp's office files instead

success.text: The swim test log for August 1957 has one line crossed out and rewritten in a kid's pencil: Mercer, J., PASSED. Beside it, in an adult's red pen, written after: Should have checked. Under the log, two memos from Director Pratt. One: Camper Mercer asking for swim lessons again. Tell her to stop pestering the staff. Girls that age just want attention. Two: Night swim, 40 campers, J. Kessler and B. Teague (age 16) supervising. Lifeguard not required. Save the expense.
success.art: A teenager reading a water-stained 1957 camp swim log by flashlight in a rusted trailer, two typed memos beside it with lines underlined in red

failure.text: The files have turned to soggy pulp. Every page you peel apart is the same printed swim-safety poster, rotted and simpering: a cartoon teen girl on a dock with hearts for eyes, EYES ON THE WATER, GIRLS. NOT ON THE BOYS. The drowned girl is on none of them. On the last one, someone has scratched JESS into the cartoon water in careful block letters.
failure.art: Soggy old file folders in a junkyard trailer revealing rotted swim-safety placards of a cartoon girl in a one-piece swimsuit and an orange life jacket waving from a dock, a name scratched into the cartoon water

clues.title: What happened on the dock
clues.hint: The school nurse at Glimmer Falls High was a junior counselor at Camp Crystal Pines in 1957. She has never once gone near the pool.

encounter.title: The Nurse's Office
encounter.text: Nurse Judy Kessler keeps a bowl of butterscotch candies, a cot with a scratchy blanket and, on the wall where she can see it from her desk, the old county swim-safety poster: a cartoon teen girl on a dock with hearts for eyes while a small shape sinks behind her, EYES ON THE WATER, GIRLS. NOT ON THE BOYS. Every September the school still hands out a pamphlet built on it. She keeps the original up. Her hands, you notice, shake whenever the water fountain in the hall runs.
encounter.art: A small high school nurse's office with a cot under a scratchy plaid blanket and a glass bowl of butterscotch candies on the desk, a middle-aged nurse with short graying hair in a cardigan sitting at the desk with shaking hands, staring at a faded printed placard on the wall of a cartoon girl in a one-piece swimsuit and a bright orange life jacket waving from a dock, a teenager sitting on the cot, flat fluorescent light, medium shot

choices.label: Ask her gently why she keeps that poster up

success.text: She is quiet a long time. "Because I'm the girl on it. I was sixteen. Bobby Teague and I had forty kids and no lifeguard, and I looked at him for one minute, because I'd never been kissed. Before that, a little girl named Jess Mercer asked me three times to teach her to float, and three times I said tomorrow." She folds her hands. "Mr. Pratt was in the lodge playing poker. He told the paper I was boy-crazy. Bobby went to college. I've spent twenty-nine years being the reason every girl in this county gets told to keep her eyes off the boys. And nobody ever says Jess's name."
success.art: A middle-aged school nurse speaking quietly at her desk with tears in her eyes, a teenager sitting on the edge of the cot listening, an old swim-team pennant on the wall between them

failure.text: Nurse Kessler's face closes like a door. "Do you have a fever? No? Then back to class." As you go, the water fountain in the hall turns on by itself and runs and runs, overflowing onto the linoleum, and behind you she starts, very quietly, to cry.
failure.art: A school hallway water fountain overflowing onto linoleum by itself, a teen walking away, a nurse's office door half closed behind them

choices.label: Fake a stomachache and lie on the cot to look around

success.text: While she gets you ginger ale, you see it in her open desk drawer: a photo of two teenagers in camp staff shirts laughing on a dock, a freckled girl in a too-big navy dress tagging behind them with a whistle, and a newspaper clipping, BOY-CRAZY COUNSELOR BLAMED IN CAMP DROWNING. Someone has written across it in red ink, decades ago: WHERE WAS THE LIFEGUARD, HARLAN? When she comes back, you tell her what you saw, and she tells you everything.
success.art: A teenager on a nurse's cot peeking into an open desk drawer at an old photo of two teen camp counselors on a dock with a freckled little girl behind them and a newspaper clipping scrawled with red ink

failure.text: She takes your temperature, and the thermometer reads 57 degrees, the temperature of a quarry lake at night. You both stare at it. The scratchy blanket on the cot is suddenly soaking wet. Nurse Kessler sends you home and locks her door.
failure.art: A nurse holding up a glass thermometer reading impossibly low, a teen on a cot under a suddenly dripping wet blanket, both staring in alarm

clues.title: Nobody had time
clues.hint: Jess Mercer is buried at the far edge of Pinecrest Cemetery. The parish register at St. Jude's lists who came to her funeral.

encounter.title: The Small Grave
encounter.text: Jess's headstone is small and tilted, at the very edge of Pinecrest where the mowers do not reach. Beside it lies her mother's, newer, with words carved too small to read from the path. Someone has left an old cork life ring leaning against Jess's stone, sun-bleached and recent. The grass around the grave is soaking wet in a perfect circle, and it is a dry October afternoon.
encounter.art: A small tilted child's headstone at the overgrown edge of a cemetery where the mowers stop, beside it a newer adult headstone covered in green moss, a sun-bleached cork life ring leaning against the small stone, a perfect circle of soaking wet grass around the grave while the rest of the ground is dry and brown, a teenager kneeling at the grave, golden October afternoon light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Ask Father Iggy to open the 1957 parish register

success.text: Iggy finds the page. Funeral of Jessamyn Mercer, age 12. Attending: her mother. One camp counselor, a girl, who stood at the back. The director sent flowers and did not attend. Her father did not attend. In the margin, in an old priest's hand: The girl never learned to swim. Her mother says she asked everyone to teach her, and nobody had time. Iggy closes the book softly. "So the poor kid was alone in the water. Then alone here, too."
success.alone: The parish office is unlocked and empty, so you find the page yourself. Funeral of Jessamyn Mercer, age 12. Attending: her mother. One camp counselor, a girl, who stood at the back. The director sent flowers and did not attend. Her father did not attend. In the margin, in an old priest's hand: The girl never learned to swim. Her mother says she asked everyone to teach her, and nobody had time. You close the book softly. Alone in the water. Then alone here, too.
success.art: A young priest in a clerical collar and band t-shirt showing a teenager a handwritten entry in an old parish register at a wooden church desk, afternoon light through stained glass

failure.text: The register is in a locked cabinet, and the key is missing. While you search, every holy water font in St. Jude's starts to overflow at once, quietly, a little lake spreading down the aisle. Iggy blesses the puddle out of habit, then hustles you outside.
failure.alone: The register is in a locked cabinet, and the key is missing. While you search, every holy water font in St. Jude's starts to overflow at once, quietly, a little lake spreading down the aisle. A sacristan comes running with a mop and hustles you outside.
failure.art: Holy water fonts overflowing in a quiet church, water spreading down the center aisle between the pews, a priest and a teen backing away

choices.label: Kneel and scrub the moss off her mother's headstone

success.text: The water soaks your knees, cold as a lake, but you keep scrubbing. The words come up out of the moss: RUTH MERCER, 1921 to 1970. And under that, the lines she chose: HER NAME WAS JESS. SHE ASKED TO LEARN TO SWIM. NOBODY HAD TIME TO TEACH HER. I WISH I HAD. As you read it, the wet circle around Jess's grave slowly soaks away into the earth.
success.art: A teenager kneeling in wet grass scrubbing moss off a headstone to reveal a heartbreaking inscription, the wet circle around a small grave beside it drying away

failure.text: The ground under your knees goes soft, then wet, then deep. For one horrible second you are up to your waist in cold black water in the middle of a cemetery. Then it is just mud, and you are just filthy, and a whistle is blowing somewhere among the mausoleums.
failure.art: A teen sunk to the waist in black water among cemetery headstones, reaching for the grass, mausoleums in the misty background

signature.title: Lights Out!
signature.place: Crystal Street, which is a lakeshore after curfew
signature.text: At midnight the storm drains on Crystal Street start running backward. By the time you reach the porch the cul-de-sac is gone: in its place lies a moonlit lakeshore, cattails where the lawns were, a wooden dock where the Delgados' driveway used to be, and a lit cabin across black water where the roundabout should be. Somebody's folding chairs and a cooler sit abandoned on the grass beside an inner tube. Then the whistle: one long blast. A woman seven feet tall wades out of the shallows, long dark hair streaming, torn navy dress dripping, a machete gleaming at her side. She pulls a cracked hockey mask down over her face. "LIGHTS OUT WAS AN HOUR AGO!" Her voice cracks on the last word like a twelve-year-old's. "Buddy check! Where's your buddy?"
signature.art: A moonlit lakeshore where a suburban cul-de-sac should be, cattails where the lawns were, a wooden dock, a lit cabin across black water, folding chairs, a cooler and an inner tube abandoned on the grass, a seven-foot muscular woman with long dark wet hair and freckled lake-pale skin wading out of the shallows in a torn soaked high-necked navy camp-staff dress with a tin whistle on a lanyard, pulling a cracked hockey mask down over her face, a dull grey machete hanging at her side, a teenager on a porch step, cold blue moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Grab the nearest friend's hand and shout "Buddy check!"

success.text: You grab a hand and hold it up high. "BUDDY CHECK!" Jess stops dead. She pushes the mask up onto her forehead to see better and looks at your joined hands for a long, strange moment, the machete hanging forgotten at her side. "Okay," she says, in a small voice. "Okay. That's the rule." She wades backward into the dark, and the lake drains away after her.
success.art: Two teens on a moonlit lakeshore holding joined hands high, a towering woman in a torn navy dress stopping short in the shallows, her cracked hockey mask pushed up on her forehead, a machete lowered at her side

failure.text: You reach for a hand, and it is not there. Your friend is three docks away, running. Jess splits the nearest folding chair in half with one swing, neat as kindling, and blows her whistle right in your face. "NO BUDDY? THEN YOU'RE ON CANOE DUTY!" You spend the rest of the night bailing your flooded basement with a saucepan, and her whistle never stops.
failure.art: A teen bailing a flooded basement with a saucepan at night, the moonlit silhouette of a towering masked woman with a machete visible through a basement window

choices.label: Splash for your front door as fast as you can

success.text: "NO RUNNING!" she roars, but you are already up your front steps, through the door and slamming it. The machete bites into the porch post once, hard enough to rattle the family photos. Then quiet. In the morning there is a deep notch in the post, a wet handprint on the door, and a single damp, folded camp rule sheet on the welcome mat.
success.art: A front porch in the morning with a deep notch cut in the wooden post, a damp folded camp rule sheet on the welcome mat, a trail of green lake weed across the steps

failure.text: You slip in the shallows and go down hard. When you look up, Jess is standing over you, dripping, the moon behind her, and she looks almost sad. "This is why we don't run," she says, and writes your name on the soggy clipboard tucked in her belt. You can feel it, after that. Being on the list.
failure.art: A teen sprawled in moonlit lake shallows looking up at a towering dripping woman in a cracked hockey mask writing their name on a soggy clipboard, a machete through her leather belt

signature.title: The Night Swim
signature.place: Crystal Street, now a lake, two a.m.
signature.text: The water is waist-deep now and the moon is enormous. Old dock posts stick up out of the roundabout, and in the middle of the lake floats a wooden swimming raft, the Heartstone glowing purple beneath it like a sunken moon. At the end of the nearest dock sit a heap of clothes, two pairs of sneakers, a cooler and a radio playing Bananarama: two teens from down the street are skinny-dipping off the end, shoulders above the water, laughing, completely oblivious. Out past them, little Petey Marchetti, nine years old, is paddling for the raft on a leaky inner tube on a dare. On the far shore, by the lit cabin, a tall masked shape lifts a machete and wades in.
signature.art: A moonlit lake covering a drowned suburban cul-de-sac at two in the morning, a wooden swim raft floating over a purple crystal glowing under the water, two teens in T-shirts swimming shoulder-deep off the end of a dock beside a heap of jeans, sneakers, a cooler and a radio, a nine-year-old boy in a striped T-shirt on a sagging inner tube paddling toward the raft, and on the far shore by a lit cabin a seven-foot woman in a hockey mask and navy dress wading in, a teenager running down the dock, wide shot

choices.label: Dive in and swim for Petey yourself

success.text: The water is shockingly cold. You reach Petey just as the tube folds under him, haul him up by the pajama collar and tow him back to the dock, coughing and furious that he did not win the dare. Jess surfaces beside you, mask pushed up, close enough to touch. She looks at you, at Petey, at the two of you together, and sinks again without a word.
success.art: A teen towing a coughing small boy in pajamas through moonlit black water to a dock, a deflated inner tube drifting away, a woman's face with a cracked hockey mask pushed up on her forehead just breaking the surface nearby, watching

failure.text: The cold punches the air out of you. Something grips your ankle, not hard, almost curiously, and pulls you under for three long seconds. When you burst back up, Petey is standing on the dock, soaked and fine, staring at you. "The big lady with the mask put me there," he says. "She said you weren't watching."
failure.art: A teen bursting up out of black moonlit water gasping, a soaked small boy safe on a dock staring at them, ripples spreading where something sank

choices.label: Yell at the skinny-dippers to look up and help

success.text: "HEY! KID IN THE WATER!" They do not hesitate. The girl kicks out for Petey, bare-shouldered and fast as a seal, and the boy shoves the cooler lid across the water like a kickboard. Together they get him up onto the dock and wrap him in somebody's beach towel. Jess, shin-deep in the shallows with the machete raised, stops. She watches the girl rub Petey's arms warm, and slowly lowers the blade, like she is seeing the end of a movie she never got to see.
success.art: Two teens in T-shirts shoulder-deep in moonlit water at the end of a dock pushing a small boy wrapped in a beach towel up onto the planks, a heap of clothes and a cooler beside them, a towering masked woman in a soaked navy dress shin-deep in the shallows, her dull grey steel machete held low and pointed at the water

failure.text: They do not hear you over the radio. They are sixteen and the moon is out. By the time you reach Petey he is sitting on the raft beside Jess, who has her mask pushed up and is showing him how to blow a tin whistle properly. They both turn and look at the skinny-dippers. Jess writes one name on her soggy clipboard: the girl's. Then she writes yours.
failure.art: A small boy in a striped T-shirt sitting on a moonlit swim raft beside a towering woman with a cracked hockey mask pushed up on her head, showing him how to blow a tin whistle, both looking toward two teens in plain white T-shirts swimming off a dock, the woman in a soaked high-necked navy dress writing on a soggy clipboard

choices.label: Rip a life ring off the old dock post and throw it

success.text: The ring is rotten cork from 1957, but it flies true, landing right in front of Petey with a splash. He grabs it, and you haul him in hand over hand. As he climbs out, the cork ring dissolves into lake mist in your hands, and from somewhere out in the dark you hear a girl's voice, cracking: "Nice throw."
success.art: A teen on a moonlit dock hauling a rope attached to an old cork life ring, a small boy clinging to it in black water, the ring beginning to dissolve into mist

failure.text: The rope is rotted through and the ring sails off into the dark alone. You have to wade in after Petey, and the water is deeper than it looks, deeper than the street could possibly be. You get him out. It takes everything you have.
failure.art: A rotted rope snapping as a life ring sails away into the moonlit dark, a teen wading neck-deep toward a small boy in black water

signature.title: The Campfire Story
signature.place: A backyard campout on Crystal Street, 11 p.m.
signature.text: Six of you are camped in the Delgados' backyard in a leaky pup tent, roasting marshmallows over a coffee-can fire. Danny Delgado holds a flashlight under his chin and starts the old story every kid in Glimmer Falls knows: the boy-crazy counselor who let a camper drown because she was too busy kissing on the dock. The flames turn a cold lake blue. Water seeps up through the grass around the fire ring. Then a seven-foot shadow steps into the circle of light, dripping, mask pushed up on her forehead, and sits down on the cooler to listen to the story about herself.
signature.art: A backyard campout at eleven at night, six kids around a coffee-can fire burning cold blue beside a sagging pup tent, a boy holding a flashlight under his chin, marshmallow sticks in hands, lake water seeping up through the grass around the fire ring, and sitting on a cooler at the edge of the light a seven-foot dripping woman in a torn navy dress with a cracked hockey mask pushed up on her forehead, listening, blue firelight on every face, wide shot

choices.label: Take the flashlight and tell the story right, with her name in it

success.text: "That's not how it goes," you say. "Her name was Jess Mercer. She was twelve. She asked three times for swim lessons and nobody had time, and the man in charge was playing poker." The fire goes from blue back to orange. Jess stares into it for a long time. Then she takes a marshmallow, roasts it perfectly, and leaves it on your stick before she wades away.
success.art: A teenager holding a flashlight and speaking earnestly by a campfire turning warm orange, a towering woman in a torn navy dress listening with her mask pushed up, one perfect golden marshmallow on a stick

failure.text: You get her name wrong. You say Jessica. The fire spits blue sparks, the tent collapses under a sudden wave of lake water, and you all spend the night wringing out sleeping bags while a whistle shrills from somewhere across the flooded lawns.
failure.art: A collapsed pup tent half-submerged in lake water in a backyard at night, soggy teenagers wringing out sleeping bags, blue sparks drifting from a sputtering fire

choices.label: Scoot over and offer her a roasting stick and a spot on the log

success.text: You scoot over and hold out a stick. Everyone freezes. Jess looks at the stick, then at the gap on the log, then at you. She sits, carefully, the log creaking under her, knees up by her ears. She burns her first marshmallow to charcoal and laughs, a cracked twelve-year-old laugh. Nobody ever saved her a seat before.
success.art: A towering woman in a torn navy dress squeezed onto a log beside teenagers at a campfire, knees up, laughing at a blackened marshmallow on her stick

failure.text: Your hand shakes and you drop the stick in the fire. Jess takes that as an answer. She stands, pulls the mask down, and blows one long blast on her whistle. "LIGHTS OUT." The fire hisses out, and nobody in the tent sleeps a wink.
failure.art: A towering masked woman in a torn navy dress standing over a hissing extinguished campfire blowing a tin whistle, terrified teenagers peering out of a pup tent in a moonlit flooded backyard

choices.label: Throw the marshmallow bag and sprint for the back door

success.text: Marshmallows fly everywhere. Jess automatically starts picking them up, because littering is against the rules, and that gives all six of you time to pile through the Delgados' sliding door and lock it. Through the glass you watch her tidy the whole campsite, roll up the tent and leave it neatly by the steps.
success.art: Teenagers crowding behind a sliding glass door at night watching a towering woman in a navy dress tidying a backyard campsite, picking up scattered marshmallows

failure.text: "NO RUNNING!" The lawn has turned to shallow lake and you belly-flop into it halfway to the door. When you surface, Jess is writing on her dripping clipboard. "Running. Littering. No buddy." She underlines the last one twice.
failure.art: A soaked teenager surfacing in a flooded backyard at night, marshmallows floating around them, a towering woman with a clipboard writing above them in the moonlight

signature.title: I'll Be Right Back
signature.place: Your house during a Crystal Street blackout, 1 a.m.
signature.text: Every light on Crystal Street goes out at once. Kev Park, sleeping over, grabs a candle. "Fuse box is in the garage. I'll be right back." Everyone in the living room turns to stare at him, because everyone has seen that movie. He goes anyway. The garage door creaks shut behind him. A thin sheet of cold lake water slides under it and across the kitchen tile, and from inside the garage comes one sharp blast of a tin whistle.
signature.art: A dark suburban living room during a blackout at one in the morning lit by a single candle on the coffee table, four teenagers on the couch and floor staring toward the kitchen where a garage door has just swung shut, a thin sheet of cold water sliding under the garage door and across the kitchen tile shining with moonlight, candlelight and blue shadow, medium wide shot

choices.label: Grab a buddy's hand and go in after him together

success.text: You go in two by two, hands locked. In the garage, ankle-deep in lake water, Kev stands at the fuse box. Jess looms behind him, holding his candle steady so he can see, mask pushed up. She looks at your joined hands and nods once, satisfied. "Nobody goes anywhere alone," she says. The lights come back on, and she is gone.
success.art: Two teenagers holding hands at a garage doorway, inside a paperboy flipping a fuse box while a towering woman in a navy dress holds a candle for him, lake water around their ankles

failure.text: Your buddy lets go in the dark. You are alone in the garage, ankle-deep in water, and Jess's mask rises up out of the shadows inches from your face. "Where's your buddy?" You do not have an answer. You spend the rest of the blackout sitting on the hood of your dad's car, being lectured about the buddy system.
failure.art: A cracked white hockey mask and long dripping dark hair emerging from the darkness of a flooded garage inches from a lone frightened teenager, lake water rippling around their ankles

choices.label: Skip the garage and throw the main breaker from the basement

success.text: The basement panel is behind the water heater. You find the main, slam it up, and the whole house blazes with light. Through the garage door you hear a startled yelp, and Kev bursts back in, soaked to the knees, holding a damp camp rule sheet. "She was RIGHT behind me," he gasps. "She told me to never go alone. Then she said please."
success.art: A teenager slamming up the main breaker on a basement electrical panel as the lights blaze on, a soaked paperboy bursting through a door behind them holding a dripping sheet of paper

failure.text: The breaker sparks and the water heater gurgles, and lake water starts pouring down the basement stairs. You wade back up to find Kev on the couch, soaked and wrapped in a towel, with no memory of the garage, holding a tin whistle he swears is not his.
failure.art: Lake water pouring down wooden basement stairs like a waterfall, a teenager wading up through it with a sparking flashlight, an electrical panel crackling beside a gurgling water heater

choices.label: Yell the rule louder than her whistle: NOBODY GOES ALONE

success.text: "NOBODY GOES ALONE!" you bellow, in your best gym-teacher voice, and the whole living room joins in. The whistle in the garage stops mid-blast. A pause. Then, from behind the door, a small cracked voice: "That's right. That's the rule." The door opens and Kev walks out, unharmed, holding a candle somebody else relit.
success.art: A living room of teenagers shouting together in candlelight at a garage door, a paperboy walking out safely holding a freshly lit candle, a glimpse of a navy dress in the shadows behind

failure.text: Your voice cracks halfway through, exactly like hers. The garage goes dead silent. Then she starts shouting the rule back at you, louder, over and over, and she keeps it up until dawn while Kev sits shivering on the workbench, too scared to move.
failure.art: A teenager mid-shout with a cracking voice in a dark candlelit living room, friends covering their ears, the garage door shuddering on its hinges, lake water rippling across the floor

signature.title: The Canoe at Dawn
signature.place: The lake that was Crystal Street, just before sunrise
signature.text: You wake up curled in the bottom of an aluminum canoe, drifting on a glassy lake where Crystal Street should be. Mist hangs over the water. The sky is going pink. A loon calls, and far off on the shore you can see porch lights and your mother in her bathrobe, waving. It is peaceful and it is beautiful, and you have seen enough movies to know exactly what happens next. The water beside the canoe begins, very gently, to bubble.
signature.art: A teenager sitting up in the bottom of a dented aluminum canoe drifting on a glassy misty lake at sunrise, pink sky, the rooftops and porch lights of a suburban street peeking out of the mist on the far shore with a woman in a bathrobe waving, gentle bubbles rising in the still water right beside the canoe, an orange life jacket on the seat, soft pink and gold light, wide shot

choices.label: Lean over the side and hold out your hand before she jumps

success.text: You lean over and put your hand flat on the water. A long, scarred arm rises out of the mist, slowly, and takes it. You help her over the side. The canoe nearly swamps, but Jess sits hunched in the bow, mask in her lap, gripping both gunwales. "I've never been in a boat," she whispers, "without being scared." You paddle her a slow circle as the sun comes up.
success.art: A towering woman in a torn navy dress hunched nervously in the bow of a canoe gripping both sides, a teenager paddling gently in the stern, a hockey mask in her lap, sunrise over a misty lake

failure.text: You reach out, and she jumps anyway, bursting from the water with a roar exactly like the end of the movie. The canoe flips. You come up sputtering on your own front lawn, which is dry, in the morning sun, with lake weed in your hair and a cold, wet handprint on your arm that takes all day to fade.
failure.art: A canoe flipping over in an explosion of lake water at dawn as a towering masked woman bursts from the surface, a teenager tumbling into the air

choices.label: Grab the paddle and race for shore

success.text: You dig in hard. The bubbles chase you across the lake, closer and closer, and the canoe slides up onto your front lawn just as a huge hand slaps the water behind you. You tumble out onto the grass. When you look back, the lake is gone, and in the dewy grass lies a waterlogged camp whistle.
success.art: A teenager paddling furiously as a canoe surges up onto a dewy suburban lawn at sunrise, a giant hand splashing the water behind, the lake mist dissolving

failure.text: The paddle snaps on the third stroke. You drift. And drift. The bubbles circle the canoe slowly, again and again, while a cracked voice under the water counts laps like a swim coach. You wake up at dawn exhausted, as if you swam the whole thing.
failure.art: A teenager in a drifting aluminum canoe holding a snapped paddle, a slow ring of bubbles circling the boat on a misty dawn lake, suburban rooftops faint in the pink haze

choices.label: Throw your orange life jacket into the bubbles

success.text: You toss it. A huge scarred hand closes on the life jacket and pulls it down. A long pause. Then it bobs back up, and Jess comes up with it, clutching it to her chest, face bare, astonished. She bobs there in the mist, held up by something for the first time, staring at you as if you are a magic trick. Then she sinks away, taking it with her.
success.art: A towering woman in a torn navy dress bobbing in a misty dawn lake clutching an orange life jacket to her chest, her face bare and astonished, a teenager watching from a canoe

failure.text: The life jacket sinks like a stone, which life jackets are not supposed to do. A second later it comes flying back out of the water and hits you in the face, followed by a blast of the whistle and a furious shout: "THAT'S NOT HOW YOU THROW IT!"
failure.art: An orange life jacket flying out of a misty lake and smacking a startled teenager in a canoe at sunrise, a splash erupting from the water

signature.title: Inspection
signature.place: The shore of Crystal Street lake, four a.m.
signature.text: Jess has made camp. Folding chairs stand in a perfect row along the moonlit waterline, a cooler serves as her podium, and every teenager on Crystal Street has been marched out of bed and lined up on the wet grass in pajamas. She paces in front of you with her mask pushed up on her head and the machete resting on her shoulder, like a drill sergeant at a summer camp in a nightmare. "Camp rules," she reads from a dripping clipboard. "Rule one: it's the girls' fault. Rule two: nobody's coming. Rule three: everyone takes the swim test." She points the machete at the raft, very far away. "Starting with you."
signature.art: Teenagers in pajamas lined up on wet grass along a moonlit lakeshore at four in the morning beside a perfectly straight row of folding chairs and a cooler, a seven-foot muscular woman with long dark wet hair in a torn high-necked navy camp-staff dress pacing in front of them with a cracked hockey mask pushed up on her head, holding up a dripping clipboard, a dull grey steel machete held low and pointed at the grass, a distant swim raft glowing purple far out on the water, blue moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Point out the rule her clipboard is missing

success.text: "You forgot Rule Zero," you say. "The grown-up in charge is responsible for the kids. Not the kids. Not the girls." Jess stares at her clipboard. She flips the page. She flips it back. Her lip trembles. "Mr. Pratt never said that one." She lets the line go back to bed, and sits alone in a folding chair at the water's edge, rereading her rules until sunrise.
success.art: A teen speaking firmly to a towering woman who stares in confusion at her clipboard, pajama-clad teens slipping away behind them toward their houses at dawn, a row of folding chairs by the water

failure.text: "That's not a rule!" Jess bellows, and her voice cracks so hard it echoes off the houses. "If that was a rule, somebody would've..." She cannot finish. She yanks the mask down and blows her whistle until dawn, and nobody on Crystal Street sleeps.
failure.art: A towering masked woman blowing a whistle furiously at a moonlit water's edge, teens covering their ears, lights on in every house

choices.label: Step out of line and refuse the swim test for everyone

success.text: "No," you say. "Nobody swims tonight. Nobody gets left in the water." The line goes silent. Then, one by one, every teen on Crystal Street steps out beside you. Jess looks at all of you standing together and the machete sinks slowly to her side. "That's," she says. "That's what counselors are supposed to say."
success.art: A line of teens in pajamas stepping forward together in defiance on a moonlit lakeshore, a towering woman in a torn navy dress staring in astonishment, her dull grey steel machete hanging low and pointed at the ground

failure.text: Your voice comes out a squeak. Jess blows her whistle. "Insubordination! Swim test, now!" You make it halfway to the raft before you wake on the shore, gasping, coughing up something that tastes like pine needles, with no idea who pulled you out.
failure.art: A teen gasping and coughing on the wet edge of a flooded street at dawn, lake weed in their hair, a tin whistle lying on the asphalt beside them

choices.label: Start singing the Camp Crystal Pines song from the rule sheet

success.text: You only know the first verse, but you belt it, and Moose joins in with a baritone like a foghorn. "Crystal Pines, oh Crystal Pines, where friendship never ends!" Jess's mouth falls open. Then, very quietly, she sings the second verse. She knows every word. By the end she is sitting on the cooler, the mask in her lap, her huge shoulders shaking.
success.alone: You only know the first verse, but you belt it like a foghorn, off-key and unashamed. "Crystal Pines, oh Crystal Pines, where friendship never ends!" Jess's mouth falls open. Then, very quietly, she sings the second verse. She knows every word. By the end she is sitting on the cooler, the mask in her lap, her huge shoulders shaking.
success.art: Teens in pajamas singing a camp song arm in arm on a moonlit lakeshore, a towering woman sitting on a cooler with her shoulders shaking, a cracked hockey mask in her lap

failure.text: Your voice cracks on the high note exactly the way hers does. Jess takes it as mockery. "Oh, you think that's FUNNY?" The whole line gets canoe duty, and you spend the night paddling a rotting canoe around the drowned cul-de-sac while she shouts strokes.
failure.art: Teens in pajamas paddling a rotting wooden canoe in circles across a moonlit lake over a drowned cul-de-sac, a towering masked woman on a dock post shouting through cupped hands

signature.title: The Pool Is Closed
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls municipal pool, closed for the season, midnight
signature.text: Kev bet Danny Delgado a dollar he would not climb the high dive at the closed-up town pool, so now four of you are over the fence at midnight. The pool was drained in September. Tonight it is full to the brim with black, cold water that smells like cattails, and the moon wobbles on the surface. The lifeguard chair stands at the edge with nobody in it, a tin whistle hanging from its arm. Danny is halfway up the high-dive ladder when you see the shape walking along the bottom of the pool, tall and slow, looking up at the unoccupied chair.
signature.art: A closed town swimming pool at midnight brimming with black cold water, moonlight wobbling on the surface, an empty tall white lifeguard chair at the edge with a tin whistle hanging from its arm, a boy halfway up the high-dive ladder, three teenagers on the deck by the fence, and deep under the water a tall dark figure walking along the bottom looking up at the empty chair, pale moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Climb up into the lifeguard chair and blow the whistle

success.text: You scramble up, grab the whistle and blow three short blasts: everybody out. Danny freezes on the ladder and climbs back down. In the water, the tall shape stops and tilts its head back, and through the black water you see a cracked hockey mask looking up at you, sitting where a grown-up should have been. It turns and walks away into the deep end, and the pool drains like a long sigh.
success.art: A teenager perched in a tall lifeguard chair blowing a tin whistle under the moon, a cracked hockey mask gazing up from beneath black pool water, a boy climbing down a high dive ladder

failure.text: The whistle is full of lake water and gargles pathetically. The shape at the bottom looks up at the chair, finds nobody there worth trusting, and starts to climb the pool ladder. All four of you go over the fence so fast that Kev leaves a sneaker behind.
failure.art: Four teenagers scrambling over a chain-link fence at night, a lone sneaker left on the pool deck, a towering dripping figure in a torn navy dress rising up the pool ladder behind them

choices.label: Talk Danny down off the high dive before anyone goes in

success.text: "Danny. The bet's off. Kev will pay you the dollar anyway, just come down." He hesitates at the top, then sees your face and climbs down rung by rung. The moment his sneakers touch concrete, the dark water goes still as glass, and a cracked voice from under the surface says, "Good. Good job."
success.art: A boy climbing carefully down a high dive ladder toward a teenager holding out a hand, the black pool below going still as glass, a faint glint of a sunken tin whistle under the moonlit surface

failure.text: "I'm not chicken!" Danny yells, and jumps. He comes up gasping and freezing but fine, and something under the water bumps his feet the whole way to the ladder. You haul him out together, all four of you shaking, and the walk home is very quiet.
failure.art: A soaked shivering boy being hauled out of a black moonlit pool by three teenagers, ripples spreading behind him, a tall dark shape gliding beneath the surface

choices.label: Drag the pool tarp back over the water and weigh it down

success.text: You grab the heavy blue tarp and drag it across, weighting the corners with lounge chairs and a trash can. The water underneath heaves once, gently, like something rolling over in bed, then goes calm. In the morning the pool is drained again, and the tarp has been folded into a perfect square, the way a camp counselor would fold it.
success.art: Teenagers hauling a heavy blue tarp across a moonlit swimming pool, lounge chairs and a trash can weighting its corners, the tarp bulging gently in the middle as if something beneath is rolling over

failure.text: The tarp slips out of your hands and sinks slowly into the black water. A hand pushes it back up and flings it onto the deck with a wet slap. Then a whistle blows from somewhere under the surface: three short blasts, which means get out.
failure.art: A soaked blue tarp flung onto a pool deck with a splash, a long scarred arm sinking back into black water, teenagers scrambling backward under the moon

signature.title: The Midnight Assembly
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls High gym, midnight
signature.text: The school bell rings at midnight, and you wake up in the gym bleachers in your pajamas with the rest of Glimmer Falls High. A filmstrip clicks on, EYES ON THE WATER, GIRLS, 1958, and a cheerful narrator explains that drownings happen when girl counselors get distracted by boys. Teachers and parents line the walls, nodding along. Lake water is seeping across the gym floor and climbing the bleachers one row at a time. At the very top, under the scoreboard, a seven-foot figure in a torn navy dress sits with her knees up, watching the film about herself.
signature.art: A dim high school gym at midnight, students in pajamas packed into the bleachers, an old filmstrip projected on a pull-down screen showing a cartoon girl on a dock, teachers and parents lining the walls nodding, dark lake water creeping up the bleacher rows, a middle-aged nurse standing by the doors with her shoes in the water, and at the very top of the bleachers a seven-foot woman in a torn navy dress sitting with her knees up, projector beam and dark shadows, wide shot

choices.label: Grab the narrator's mic and tell the filmstrip the right way

success.text: You step up to the projector and talk right over the narrator. "And here is Director Harlan Pratt, playing poker in the lodge instead of hiring a lifeguard." The gym laughs, at him for once. "And here is Jess Mercer, age twelve, who asked for swim lessons three times." The water stops climbing, and at the top of the bleachers the figure leans forward, mask in her hands, listening to her own name in front of the whole school.
success.art: A teenager speaking into a microphone beside a clattering filmstrip projector in a dark gym, students in pajamas laughing, lake water halted at the bottom row, a towering figure at the top of the bleachers leaning forward with a hockey mask in her hands

failure.text: The narrator's voice gets louder and louder until it drowns yours out: EYES ON THE WATER, GIRLS. The teachers shush you. The water reaches the third row, and you wake up with wet pajama cuffs.
failure.art: Teachers shushing a teenager standing at a filmstrip projector in a dark gym, a cheerful 1950s narrator image glowing on the screen, black water lapping at the third row of bleachers

choices.label: Climb the wall and tear down the old swim-safety notice

success.text: That warning has hung by the gym doors since 1958. You climb the end of the bleachers, grab a corner and rip it down the middle with a sound like a slap. The filmstrip sputters, and the water stops at your ankles. Up under the scoreboard, Jess stands up very slowly, and through the cracked mask you think you see the corner of a smile.
success.art: A teenager at the end of the bleachers ripping a faded old swim-safety notice off a gym wall, torn paper fluttering down, a filmstrip sputtering on the screen, a towering woman in a soaked navy dress and a cracked hockey mask rising slowly under the scoreboard

failure.text: It will not tear. The paper stretches like wet taffy and snaps back flat, and the lake water surges up two rows at once. A whistle blows from the top of the bleachers, one long blast, and every kid in the gym lifts their feet.
failure.art: A teenager straining to tear a stubborn faded notice off a gym wall, black water surging up the bleachers, students in pajamas lifting their feet, a towering woman in a soaked navy dress and a cracked hockey mask blowing a tin whistle at the top

choices.label: Go sit beside Nurse Kessler, who is shaking by the doors

success.text: Nurse Kessler stands by the gym doors, white as chalk, her shoes already in the water. You sit beside her on the bottom bleacher and take her hand. "I was sixteen," she whispers. You tell her it was never a sixteen-year-old's job to be the only grown-up at the lake, and she grips your hand hard as the water slides back off the gym floor like a tide going out.
success.art: A teenager sitting on the bottom bleacher holding the hand of a pale middle-aged school nurse in a cardigan, dark water retreating across a gym floor like a tide, a filmstrip glowing faintly behind them

failure.text: She flinches away from you. "Not now," she says. "Not here." She walks out of the gym into the dark hallway, the water follows her, and the filmstrip starts over from the beginning.
failure.art: A pale school nurse in a cardigan walking away down a dark school hallway, a trail of lake water following her out of a gym, a filmstrip restarting on the screen behind a lone teenager

signature.title: The Lodge
signature.place: The Camp Crystal Pines lodge, risen on the roundabout, midnight the night before Halloween
signature.text: A thunderstorm rolls over Crystal Street the night before Halloween, and when the lightning flashes, the Camp Crystal Pines lodge is standing on the roundabout, dripping, risen whole out of 1957. Inside, the fire is lit and a poker game is frozen mid-hand: four grown men in short sleeves, cards fanned, cigar smoke hanging in the air, and at the head of the table Director Harlan Pratt, chuckling at nothing. The lodge clock reads 9:58, two minutes before the night swim went wrong. Someone is pounding on the front door hard enough to rattle the antlers on the wall, and a cracked voice outside is shouting, "Let me in! Nobody's watching the water!"
signature.art: A rustic summer camp lodge at night during a thunderstorm, a crackling stone fireplace, antlers on the log wall, four grown men in short-sleeved shirts frozen around a poker table with playing cards fanned in their hands and cigar smoke hanging in the air, an old wall clock with its hands just before ten, a teenager standing at the heavy front door with a hand on the bolt as the door shakes from pounding outside, white lightning in the windows, warm firelight, wide shot

choices.label: Slide back the bolt and let her in out of the storm

success.text: You slide back the bolt. Jess ducks through the doorway, enormous and soaked, rain sheeting off her dress, and stops, staring at the warm room she was never allowed into. You pull a chair up to the fire for her. She sits, carefully, and holds her scarred hands out to the flames, and the frozen men at the poker table flicker and fade like smoke up the chimney.
success.art: A towering soaked woman in a torn navy dress seated by a lodge fireplace holding her scarred hands to the flames, a teenager pulling up beside her, ghostly poker players fading like smoke behind them

failure.text: You open the door and the storm comes in with her: wind, rain and lake water all at once, knocking you flat. Jess looks around the lodge, sees the poker table, and pulls her mask down. She goes back out into the storm, and the door slams behind her.
failure.art: A storm blasting through an open lodge door, a teenager knocked flat by a wave of rain and lake water, a towering masked woman turning away from a poker table into the lightning

choices.label: Haul on the lodge alarm bell: lifeguard to the waterfront

success.text: There is a brass bell by the door with a frayed rope beneath it. You haul on it, and the bell nobody rang in 1957 clangs out across the lake, again and again. The poker players look up, startled, for the first time in twenty-nine years. Outside, the pounding stops, and the clock ticks past ten with the whole lodge listening.
success.art: Inside a log lodge during a thunderstorm, a teenager hauling on the rope of a big brass bell by the open door, ghostly poker players at a green card table looking up startled, an old wall clock past ten

failure.text: The bell rope comes apart in your hands, rotten from twenty-nine years underwater. The clock strikes ten. Outside, the pounding stops, and the silence is worse.
failure.art: A teenager staring at a snapped rotten bell rope in their hands inside a firelit lodge, a wall clock striking ten, rain streaming down the dark windows

choices.label: Flip the poker table and drag the director down to the dock

success.text: Cards, chips and cigars go flying. You grab Director Pratt by his short-sleeved collar and haul him, sputtering, out into the rain and down to the end of the dock. "Look," you tell him. "Forty kids. No lifeguard. Look at the water." For the first time, the memory of Harlan Pratt looks, and sees, and his face crumples, and the whole lodge folds into the lake behind you like a house of cards.
success.art: A teenager dragging a sputtering middle-aged man in short sleeves down a rain-lashed wooden dock toward black water, playing cards whirling in the wind, a rustic lodge collapsing into the lake behind them

failure.text: The table will not budge, bolted to the floor by twenty-nine years of habit. Pratt deals you a hand without looking up. "Sit down, kid. The girls will handle it." You hear the clock tick toward ten.
failure.art: A smug middle-aged man in short sleeves dealing cards to a teenager straining against a heavy bolted poker table, a lodge clock ticking toward ten, a storm flashing at the windows

finale.title: The Last Night Swim
finale.place: Crystal Springs lake, which is Crystal Street, Halloween night
finale.text: On Halloween night the lake comes all the way back. Moonlight pours over black water lapping at the porch roofs of Crystal Street, jack-o'-lanterns bob past a drifting cooler and a tangle of folding chairs, and the old raft rides over the drowned Heartstone, glowing purple from below. Every teen in Glimmer Falls is treading water around it in their Halloween costumes, too cold to scream. Jess stands on the raft, mask down, machete raised to the moon. "Nobody watched me," she says, and her voice is twelve years old. "Nobody even says my name. They just tell girls to keep their eyes off the boys. So nobody gets out of the water. Not until somebody watches."
finale.art: A suburban cul-de-sac completely flooded under a full moon on Halloween night, black water lapping at the porch roofs, jack-o'-lanterns, a cooler and folding chairs floating past, a wooden swim raft glowing purple from a sunken crystal below, a seven-foot muscular woman in a torn high-necked navy dress and a cracked hockey mask standing on the raft with a dull grey steel machete held low and pointed at the water, teens in Halloween costumes treading water around her, cold moonlight and purple glow, wide shot

choices.label: Swim for the raft and wrestle the machete away from her

success.text: You haul yourself onto the raft, grab her wrist with both hands and twist until the machete spins away into the lake. Without it, Jess staggers, slips and falls back with an enormous splash. The water goes with her, pouring down every storm drain on Crystal Street at once like a bathtub draining, and you are left standing on a wooden raft in the middle of a dry roundabout.
success.art: A teen gripping both hands around the wrist of a towering woman in a soaked high-necked navy dress and a cracked hockey mask on a moonlit raft as her machete spins away into the lake and she topples backward into the water, black floodwater swirling down storm drains, the street draining dry

failure.text: She is too big and too strong and she has been underwater a very long time. She lifts you off the raft by your costume like a kitten and sets you back in the water. "Swim test," she says, and the lake closes over your head.
failure.art: A towering masked woman holding a teen by the back of their costume over moonlit black water, about to set them down, the purple glow of a sunken geode below

choices.label: Blow the camp's all-out-of-the-water signal on her own whistle

success.text: You snatch the tin whistle off her belt and blow three short blasts, the signal printed on every Camp Crystal Pines rule sheet: swim is over, everybody out. It is the only rule Jess never got to hear. She freezes. Every teen kicks for the porches. And Jess, by habit, by rule, turns and wades out of the water too, into the dark between the houses, and is gone.
success.art: A teen on a moonlit raft blowing a tin whistle, costumed teens swimming for porches, a towering masked woman turning obediently to wade away into darkness between houses

failure.text: The whistle is full of lake water and gurgles pathetically. Jess laughs, a horrible cracking laugh, and takes it back. "Nobody blows my whistle." She blows it herself: one long blast, which means everybody under.
failure.art: A teen blowing a waterlogged tin whistle that only gurgles, a towering masked woman laughing and reaching to take it back, black water rising under the moon

choices.label: Say her name, form a buddy line, swim out to her and teach her to float

success.text: You hold up her swim card, Judy's story and her mother's words, and you say it out loud: "Jess." Then you do what nobody did in 1957: you get in the water with her. Your crew links hands, porch to raft, a human chain. Nurse Judy Kessler wades in at the end of it in her coat, into lake water for the first time in twenty-nine years. You take Jess's enormous cold hand. "It wasn't your fault," you say. "And it wasn't Judy's, or any girl's. Lie back. We've got you. You're not alone in the water." The machete slides from her fingers and sinks. Slowly she pushes the mask up, then off, and lets it float away. Then, shaking, Jess lies back on the black lake, and a dozen hands hold her up.
success.art: A human chain of teens in Halloween costumes linking hands from a porch to a raft across moonlit black water, a nurse in a coat wading in at the end, a towering woman in a torn navy dress floating on her back held up by many hands, her cracked hockey mask drifting away, the sunken geode glowing purple below

failure.text: You reach for her hand and she flinches away and yanks the mask back down. "Nobody gets in the water with me. Nobody ever has." She sinks out of reach, and the lake rises another foot. You have the truth, but she does not believe yet that anyone will stay.
failure.art: A towering masked woman flinching away from a teen's outstretched hand and sinking into moonlit black water, the flood rising around a broken human chain

choices.label: Shout "BUDDY CHECK!" across the whole lake, the rule that stopped her that first week

success.text: That first week taught you that Jess cannot ignore a camp rule, any more than she can stop being twelve. So you cup your hands and bellow across the black water, "BUDDY CHECK!" Every teen in the lake grabs a hand and holds it high, pairs and pairs and pairs, and Jess has to count them, porch by porch and raft by raft, mask pushed up so she can see. When she finishes, nobody is missing, and the girl nobody counted lowers her machete, blows three soft blasts that mean swim's over, and wades away into the dark as the water drains after her.
success.art: Dozens of costumed teenagers treading moonlit water and holding joined hands high in pairs, a towering woman in a torn navy dress on a raft counting them with her hockey mask pushed up, porch roofs poking above the lake

failure.text: "BUDDY CHECK!" Half the teens in the water are too cold to lift their hands. Jess counts, comes up short, and her shoulders sag under the dripping dress. "See," she says. "Somebody always gets left."
failure.art: Shivering costumed teenagers treading black water around a raft, only a few hands raised, a towering masked woman on the raft with slumped shoulders, jack-o'-lanterns bobbing past

choices.label: Rally every teen in the water to shout her rule down: we watch out for each other now

success.text: Midweek you watched teenagers prove the town wrong: skinny-dippers who swam for a little kid, friends who went into a dark garage in pairs, a gym full of kids who finally heard who really left the lake unwatched. So you shout it across the black water, and every teen treading water shouts it back: "WE WATCH EACH OTHER NOW!" They link arms and kick together, a raft of costumes pushing back against her raft, until Jess staggers with the machete drooping and her rule broken in front of her. With a long, cracked wail she sinks off the raft, and the lake pours down every storm drain on Crystal Street after her.
success.art: A huge ring of costumed teenagers linking arms in moonlit water and shouting together, pushing toward a wooden raft, a towering masked woman in a soaked navy dress staggering backward, her dull grey steel machete hanging low and pointed at the water, water swirling down toward storm drains

failure.text: Your shout breaks against the cold. A few teens try to link arms, but their teeth chatter too hard to say the words. Jess shakes her head slowly. "That's what they always say," she says, "right before they look away."
failure.art: A few shivering costumed teenagers trying to link arms in black water, a towering masked woman on a raft shaking her head slowly, moonlight on drowned porch roofs

choices.label: Say her name, hold out the hand she trusted the night before Halloween, and float with her

success.text: The night before Halloween you showed her that somebody stays, so you do it again, out loud, in front of the whole town. "Jess," you say, and slide off the porch into the black water and swim for the raft, your crew linking hands behind you, porch to raft, with Nurse Judy Kessler wading in at the end of the chain. You hold out your hand, the same hand that reached for her before. "It wasn't your fault, or Judy's, or any girl's. Lie back. We've got you." The machete sinks, the mask floats away, and Jess lies back on the lake with a dozen hands holding her up, and floats.
success.art: A towering scarred woman in a torn navy dress floating on her back on a moonlit lake, a dozen hands of costumed teenagers holding her up, a middle-aged nurse in a coat waist-deep at the end of a human chain, a hockey mask drifting away

failure.text: She reaches for your hand, then the cold and the old fear win, and she pulls back under her mask. "Not yet," she whispers. "Everybody says they'll stay." She was so close.
failure.art: A towering masked woman on a raft pulling her scarred hand back from a costumed teenager treading water, moonlight on the black lake, a human chain of friends stretching back to a porch

best.title: Buddy Check
best.text: Jess floats. For the first time in her life, or after it, she floats, and she starts to laugh, a twelve-year-old's laugh, high and astonished. As she laughs she grows smaller and the scars fade, until the hands are holding up a skinny freckled girl in a too-big navy dress with a tin whistle. Judy Kessler takes the faded staff patch off her old camp jacket and pins it on Jess's collar. "Counselor Jess," she says. "I'm sorry I said tomorrow." Jess salutes her, and the whole lake drains away like a long sigh, leaving dew on every lawn, a raft on the roundabout and a cracked hockey mask lying empty in a puddle. That winter every EYES ON THE WATER, GIRLS poster in the county comes down. Next summer the Glimmer Falls public pool opens the Jess Mercer Learn-to-Swim Program, free for every kid, with a sign at the gate that says GROWN-UPS: WATCH THE WATER. Its first three lifeguards are teenage girls. Judy teaches the first class.
best.art: A skinny freckled twelve-year-old girl ghost in a too-big navy dress with a tin whistle floating on her back on a moonlit lake and laughing, held up by many hands of teens in Halloween costumes, a middle-aged nurse in the water pinning a faded camp staff patch on her collar, an empty cracked hockey mask drifting away, pink dawn breaking over the roofs of a suburban cul-de-sac, wide shot

good.title: Swim's Over
good.text: The lake drains down the storm drains at dawn and Crystal Street dries out by lunch, leaving a raft on the roundabout that nobody can explain. The town calls it a water main break. The poster in Nurse Kessler's office stays on the wall, and the pamphlet goes out again in September. Every so often, at the high school pool, a lifeguard swears she saw a tall woman in a cracked hockey mask standing in the deep end, watching.
good.art: A dry suburban roundabout at sunrise, a waterlogged wooden swim raft sitting on the grass beside a purple crystal rock, a cracked hockey mask resting on the raft, puzzled neighbors in bathrobes and slippers gathered around it holding coffee mugs, damp lawns shining, gold morning light, wide shot

bittersweet.title: High Water Mark
bittersweet.text: Jess goes back under, and the water goes with her, but not all the way. Every basement on Crystal Street stays a little damp. Every Halloween after, the storm drains gurgle at midnight, the moon comes up too big, and the water rises an inch, then two, then stops. Nurse Kessler retires that spring without ever taking down the poster, and still nobody in town says Jess's name.
bittersweet.art: A damp suburban basement at night with a faint dark waterline on the wood-paneled wall, cardboard boxes stacked on bricks, and through the small basement window a moonlit street where a storm drain gurgles beside a glowing jack-o'-lantern on the curb, a teenager on the basement stairs looking at the waterline, blue moonlight, medium shot

bad.title: Swim Lessons
bad.text: The lake drains away at dawn and takes you with it, not drowned but Taken, down into a night swim that never ends. Every Halloween after, when the storm drains run backward and the moonlit water rises over Crystal Street, your crew sees you under the surface: in a faded staff t-shirt with a tin whistle, standing beside a towering woman in a cracked hockey mask, lining up teenagers who are not watching each other. You look like you are blowing your whistle. Nobody can hear it.
bad.art: Black moonlit floodwater over a suburban street, and under the surface the pale figures of a teenager in a faded camp staff T-shirt with a tin whistle standing beside a seven-foot woman in a torn navy dress and a cracked hockey mask, three worried friends kneeling on a porch roof and peering down into the water, white moonlight, high angle shot
